opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is really where the whole thing clicks for me. The way I see it, most of the interesting problems in machine learning are fundamentally probabilistic. You want a distribution over hypotheses, not just a point estimate. You want to know what you don't know. And Bayesian inference is the principled way to do that, but in practice it's brutally expensive on conventional hardware. You end up running Markov chain Monte Carlo or Langevin dynamics, and you're simulating randomness with pseudo-random number generators on deterministic digital circuits that are spending enormous amounts of energy to suppress noise in the first place. It's kind of absurd when you think about it. We pay to remove noise at the transistor level, and then we pay again in software to put noise back in.

With thermodynamic computing, the idea is to flip that around. Nature is already sampling. A physical system in contact with a heat bath naturally relaxes toward a Boltzmann distribution, where the probability of a state goes like e to the minus energy over kT. If you can engineer the energy landscape of your hardware so that it encodes the posterior or the model you care about, then the physics just does the sampling for you. Langevin dynamics isn't something you simulate anymore. It's literally what the circuit is doing. The noise is a resource rather than a nuisance.

So there's a really natural mapping. Things like Gaussian sampling, matrix inversion through relaxation to equilibrium, diffusion-style generative models, energy-based models, all of these have a very direct physical instantiation. And what excites me is that you potentially get orders of magnitude gains in speed and energy efficiency for exactly the class of algorithms that we've historically shied away from because they were too costly.

More broadly, I think it reframes what intelligence even is computationally. A lot of what we're doing with AI is learning and sampling from distributions, and the universe is fundamentally a big stochastic, thermodynamic process. So building hardware that's native to that, rather than fighting it, feels like the right direction to me. It's about aligning the substrate of computation with the physics, and Bayesian inference is the cleanest place where that alignment pays off.

r001.rationale: It says the hardware’s energy landscape can be engineered to encode the posterior or model, describing a programmable energy function.

r002.rationale: It says Langevin dynamics is performed by the circuit itself and that the physics samples the encoded distribution, identifying native physical sampling for Bayesian inference.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The thing I find compelling is that Bayesian inference is, at its heart, a thermodynamic problem that we've been forcing onto hardware that was never built for it. When you do posterior sampling, what you really want is a system whose equilibrium distribution is your posterior. Nature does this for free. A physical system coupled to a heat bath relaxes to a Boltzmann distribution, and if you can engineer the energy landscape so that the Boltzmann distribution matches the distribution you care about, then thermalization is sampling. You just let the system sit, and the noise does the work.

On a digital computer, we fake this. We take deterministic transistors, spend enormous energy suppressing the thermal noise that's naturally there, and then burn more cycles generating pseudorandom numbers to reinject the stochasticity we just removed. Langevin dynamics, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, diffusion models, all of these are simulations of a physical process. So the question we asked was: why simulate it? Why not build a circuit whose actual physics is the Langevin equation you'd otherwise be integrating step by step?

That's what our thermodynamic chips do. They're analog stochastic circuits where the noise is a resource rather than an enemy. For the simplest case, a Gaussian posterior, you can map the precision matrix onto a network of coupled oscillators or RC elements, and the stationary distribution of the voltages is exactly the Gaussian you want. So linear algebra primitives that show up everywhere in Bayesian methods, matrix inversion, solving linear systems, Gaussian sampling, become physical relaxation processes. The scaling is really nice because the physics does the whole matrix at once in parallel, instead of iterating.

Where it gets more interesting is going beyond Gaussians, to the kinds of multimodal, high-dimensional posteriors you hit in Bayesian deep learning or in generative models. Even there, the structure holds. Diffusion models are literally reverse-time stochastic differential equations. Energy-based models are Boltzmann distributions. So there's a very natural fit between the mathematics people are already using and what this hardware does natively, and that alignment is what makes me think this isn't just a curiosity but a real computational substrate.

And then there's a deeper point I keep coming back to, which is that intelligence itself might be best understood thermodynamically. Learning is a system reducing its free energy with respect to its environment. Inference is the same thing on a faster timescale. If that's the right frame, then building machines that compute by physically relaxing toward equilibrium isn't a hack, it's closer to how the problem should have been posed all along. Digital computing was the detour.

r001.rationale: The response says the energy landscape can be engineered to match a desired distribution, but it does not clearly characterize the chip as a programmable energy function.

r002.rationale: It describes the chip’s physical dynamics as the Langevin equation and explains that thermalization samples the desired posterior distribution, conveying a physical implementation of sampling for Bayesian inference.

astra-6.text:
What I find compelling is that Bayesian inference is fundamentally about distributions, and thermodynamics gives you a physical way to represent and sample distributions. Instead of treating the fluctuations in a chip as noise you have to suppress, you can try to make them do useful computational work.

The connection is through energy. If you can encode the negative log of a posterior distribution as an energy landscape, then the equilibrium distribution of that system corresponds to the posterior, with temperature setting the relevant scale. So the algorithm and the physics start to look like two descriptions of the same process.

But the interesting challenge is getting the dynamics right. Having the right equilibrium distribution doesn’t mean you can reach it efficiently. You can get stuck in a mode, just as a software sampler can. That’s why I find the co-design compelling: you’re designing the chip and the inference algorithm together, so the physical dynamics help you explore the distribution you actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response says the posterior’s negative log can be encoded as an energy landscape and describes designing the chip and inference algorithm together, conveying a configurable energy function.

r002.rationale: It describes physical fluctuations sampling a distribution, but does not identify the chip’s native dynamics as Langevin-like or explicitly connect them to MCMC sampling.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find compelling is that Bayesian inference is fundamentally about distributions, whereas we’ve built most of our computers to give us very precise, deterministic answers. We then spend a lot of computation generating randomness and using it to explore a posterior distribution.

With a thermodynamic chip, the idea is to make that exploration part of the physics. You encode a probability distribution into an energy landscape, and the system’s fluctuations help it explore possible configurations. Ideally, low-energy configurations correspond to hypotheses that have high posterior probability. So noise becomes a computational resource.

The interesting challenge is making those dynamics useful: can you encode the problem faithfully, move between different modes, and get representative samples quickly? Reaching equilibrium and sampling efficiently aren’t automatically the same thing. That’s where the hardware and the inference algorithm really have to be designed together.

r001.rationale: The response says a probability distribution is encoded into an energy landscape, which conveys configuring the chip’s energy function.

r002.rationale: It describes physical fluctuations exploring configurations and sampling, but does not identify Langevin-like dynamics or characterize them as an implementation of MCMC.
